title: AI Will Not Fix CPD. It May Show Us What CPD Avoids
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes opens with a vignette of an experienced teacher, Claire, sitting through a CPD session whose strategy dissolves by the next morning, then turns to a review of 20 studies on generative AI in teacher professional development. She welcomes the review's awkward conclusion that AI supports teacher learning only when CPD is built around judgement, critique, collaboration and ethics. Working through its four uses (functional, cognitive, social and reflective), she argues that AI's real value is giving departments concrete material to disagree with, such as hinge questions or rival explanations to tear apart. Because generative AI can produce fluent, confident nonsense, she contends that it raises rather than reduces the value of teacher subject expertise. She warns school leaders against confusing warm responses with impact and against turning AI into a launch, platform or glossy slide deck. Her closing claim is that the value of AI in CPD is not answers but better material to question.
points: Hughes's central claim is that AI in CPD is useful only when it gives teachers concrete material to critique, turning training from 'use AI to save time' into 'use AI to create better professional argument.'
Because generative AI can be fluent, polite and wrong, she argues it raises the value of teacher expertise: novices may accept plausible outputs that stronger teachers can see are missing a step.
She recommends starting CPD from professional problems (a failed lesson, weak assessment responses, a common misconception) rather than prompts, then having departments evaluate AI outputs together.
Leaders should judge AI-enabled CPD by changes in planning, questioning, pupil writing and feedback precision, not by teacher confidence, which is cheap to measure and easy to misread.
She adopts the review's sequence of exploration, integration, critique and exchange, and warns that schools may otherwise produce a situation where everyone gets trained and no one gets wiser.
quotes: This is why this paper I recently read on generative AI and teacher development caught my attention. It isn’t a promise of rescue, but it reviews 20 studies on generative AI in teacher professional development and reaches a more awkward conclusion than the sales pitch often offered around AI: the tools can support teacher learning, but only when schools build CPD around judgement, critique, collaboration and ethics. Good!
At this point, AI has not replaced the teacher. It has given the department something concrete to disagree with. Useful, yes.
The cognitive promise is more interesting. The review suggests AI can support problem-solving, higher-order thinking and metacognition. I would be careful here.
It can offer feedback which is fluent, polite and useless. Fluent and useless is already a problem in education. We do not need more of it.

A novice teacher may accept an attractive output since it sounds right. A stronger teacher can see the missing step, the muddy explanation, the weak example, the careless task. AI raises the value of teacher expertise.
So school leaders need better evidence of impact than warm responses. Did planning improve? Did questions become sharper?
But the professional act remains with the teacher. Perhaps the real value of AI in CPD is not answers. It gives us better material to question.
